summary: Documents experience with OSPF version 2, including interoperability testing, field experience, simulations, and the state of implementations. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a report on how the router map-sharing system did when people tried it in real life.

subtitle: An operational report on the OSPF routing protocol's performance in real-world deployments.

tldr.problem: The OSPF v2 routing protocol had been developed but needed to demonstrate interoperability, security design, and real-world operational experience before advancing to Draft Standard status.
tldr.mechanism: This document reports on OSPF v2 testing across multiple independent implementations, security architecture with packet authentication, and operational deployments across NASA, regional networks and research institutions.
tldr.outcome: The report demonstrated that OSPF v2 was well-specified enough for independent interoperable implementations, had robust authentication, and performed significantly better than RIP in production networks with faster convergence and lower bandwidth consumption.

today: RFC 1246 is an Informational RFC from July 1991 that documents the experience leading up to OSPF v2 advancement to Draft Standard status. OSPF v2 eventually became a full Internet Standard (STD 54). The protocol remains widely used in modern networks, though it has been supplemented and extended with additional RFCs such as RFC 2328 (the current OSPF v2 specification) and extensions for IPv6 (OSPFv3).

sections.title: Purpose and Background
sections.content:
RFC 1246 documents the operational experience with OSPF Version 2, an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) used for routing within large networks called Autonomous Systems. This report was required by the IETF standards body for OSPF v2 to advance from Proposed Standard to Draft Standard status. The requirements for advancement include clear specification, a Management Information Base (MIB), demonstrated security, multiple independent interoperable implementations, and significant operational experience in production networks.

OSPF Version 1 was published in RFC 1131, and Version 2 addressed several limitations found in Version 1. This document focuses exclusively on OSPF Version 2 deployed between 1990 and early 1991 across multiple research networks and commercial deployments. The report compiles information about interoperability testing, security mechanisms, implementation status, and real-world performance observations from sites including NASA's Science Internet, regional academic networks, and research institutions.
sections.eli5: This paper proves OSPF is ready for the major leagues: different companies built it the same way and got them all talking to each other, the security works, and real networks love it.

sections.title: Specification and Management Framework
sections.content:
OSPF Version 2 is formally specified in RFC 1247. The protocol is well-documented enough that independent organizations developed compatible implementations without consulting the original creators. All OSPF packet exchanges include a 16-bit Authentication type field and 64 bits of Authentication data in the packet header. Different OSPF areas can use different authentication schemes; the current assignments are Type 0 (no authentication) and Type 1 (simple password authentication), with types 2-255 reserved for future assignment and types above 255 available for local per-Autonomous System definitions.

OSPF v2 is supported by a comprehensive Management Information Base published in RFC 1248. The MIB includes 105 objects organized into a general variables group and ten tables: area descriptions, stub area configurations, the link state database, area range specifications, directly connected hosts, interface variables, interface metrics by type of service, virtual links, neighbors, and virtual neighbors. This MIB provides network administrators with detailed monitoring and configuration capabilities.
sections.eli5: The protocol is written down clearly, the security is defined (messages can be password-checked), and there is a standard way to measure and control the router using network management tools.

sections.title: Security Architecture and Authentication
sections.content:
Authentication is mandatory in OSPF. When a router receives an OSPF packet from a network, it first verifies that the packet indicates the correct Authentication type. The router then authenticates the packet by running a verification algorithm that uses the configured authentication key, the 64-bit Authentication data field, and the rest of the packet as input. Packets failing authentication are dropped, and the failure is logged in a MIB-accessible variable for monitoring.

The RFC documents that OSPF allows authentication to be configured on a per-network basis, which gives administrators flexibility in managing security keys across different network segments. Type 1 (simple password) authentication has been deployed in production, though more sophisticated authentication types were expected to be added in future OSPF extensions.
sections.eli5: OSPF makes every router prove it is who it says it is by checking a password. If a router fails the check, the message is thrown away. No fake routers allowed.

sections.title: Implementations and Interoperability Testing
sections.content:
The report documents five major OSPF v2 implementations that participated in interoperability testing: 3com, ACC (based on University of Maryland code), Proteon, Wellfleet, and the University of Maryland implementation. The implementations range from about 9,000 to 24,000 lines of C code (excluding user interface and MIB code). Of these, the implementations from 3com, Proteon, and the University of Maryland were developed independently of each other, satisfying the requirement for multiple independent interoperable implementations.

The 3com implementation was the only one to implement OSPF's Type of Service (TOS) routing feature. The ACC implementation was the only one with a working OSPF MIB implementation at the time. Proteon's implementation had the most significant field experience. All implementations participated in multiple rounds of interoperability testing, demonstrating that the OSPF v2 specification was clear enough for independent vendors to build compatible systems.
sections.eli5: Five different companies built OSPF, and we tested them all talking to each other. They worked together perfectly, proving the spec is clear.

sections.title: Real-World Deployment and Performance
sections.content:
By the time of this report, OSPF v2 was deployed across multiple production networks. Three major deployments are documented in detail:

  • NASA Science Internet (NSI): 15 routers deployed using the Proteon implementation, with 496 external routes imported from RIP and EGP. NSI's testing showed OSPF convergence time of about 3 seconds when a link fails and routing resumes, compared to minutes for RIP. OSPF consumed many times less network bandwidth than RIP.
  • BARRNet (NSFNet regional network): 14 OSPF routers with a redundant ring core topology, deployed in April 1990 and upgraded to v2 in November 1990, importing 1816 external routes.
  • OARnet (Ohio Academic Resources Network): 13 OSPF routers deployed starting October 1990, running with RIP routes imported. Testing showed routes re-synchronized in about 2 seconds when a circuit failed, compared to 3-6 minutes for RIP.

Field experience from OARnet's Event Logging System demonstrated that routes converged within seconds when links flapped or came back up. The protocol effectively handled the complex task of importing external routes and adapting to network topology changes.
sections.eli5: Real networks used OSPF and it worked great: when a link broke, it found a new route in 2-3 seconds. RIP took several minutes. And OSPF used way less bandwidth.

sections.title: Evolution and Deployment Timeline
sections.content:
OSPF Version 1 began deployment in Spring 1990, with initial results reported to the ospf-tests mailing list. No protocol bugs were found in this initial deployment, but several features were identified as desirable and added to Version 2. OSPF Version 2 began field trials in 1990 and was deployed in production networks in various organizations starting in April 1990 for NSI and BARRNet, and October 1990 for OARnet. The protocol also expanded to commercial networks; 3com deployed OSPF on their corporate network with plans to cut over all routers from RIP.

The initial deployment experience showed that OSPF was robust in practice. The early identification of missing features (such as the forwarding address for external LSAs and stub areas) through real-world use led to improvements that were incorporated into OSPF v2 before this report was published, demonstrating a healthy development process responsive to operational needs.
sections.eli5: OSPF started in 1990 and people found a few things that needed improvement. Those got added to version 2, and then lots of networks switched to it and loved it.
